## What never goes into the cockpit

Not in reports, not in learnings, not shortened or "just the start":

- **Secrets:** tokens (Jira/Atlassian, GitHub), passwords, private keys,
  encryption passwords, cookies, URLs with
  embedded credentials.
- **Anything from `.env`** and similar files.
- **Customer data:** Testdata test customers (phone number, postcode, date of
  birth, name), customer and contract numbers, IMEI, e-mail addresses,
  anything from production data. Describe the kind instead: "a
  Renewal-capable test customer from Testdata".

The routine refuses obvious secrets with 400 "Text apparently contains a
secret (…) — not stored.", mobile numbers too ("phone number"). That is a
safety net, not a check: other customer data it does not see at all. On this
refusal drop the secret entirely and phrase the text without it; a masked,
split, re-encoded or starred copy stores exactly what the net is there to
stop. The one exception is a false alarm in prose without a secret (say
"Password: never in the log" trips the password rule): just rephrase it
("passwords never go into the log").

## Routine unreachable

No output with exit code 7, 28, 52 or 56 (connection refused, 5 seconds up,
empty reply, connection reset) means the routine is restarting: it is back
within a few minutes. The wait block rides that out on its own. Any other
call you repeat once with curl's own retry, the flags after the URL (the
prefix stays what the permission rule targets), no loop and no `sleep`:

```bash
curl -s --max-time 5 https://routine-utt5l6k4qa-ez.a.run.app/api/cockpit/request/12/answer -G -d arbeit=42 --retry 60 --retry-connrefused --retry-delay 5 --retry-max-time 300
```

For a POST the same flags go after the URL, before `-H`. Only when the retry
still fails after five minutes, or the `curl` was not approved, is the
cockpit out for this session:

- **work on**: the task comes first;
- **say it once**, in one sentence: "The cockpit is unreachable, I stop
  reporting for this session.";
- **stop calling the cockpit** for the rest of the session: no further retry,
  no attempt to start the routine yourself.

Create the work item once more via `POST /arbeit` and report on with the
answer's `id` when someone says the cockpit runs again (it finds the old one),
on a 400/404 "Unknown work item." (the `id` is stale) and on a 409 "Work item
is archived." (it was confirmed done and archived meanwhile).

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Consensus
Consensus is a research paper search engine: relevance-ranked semantic search over 400M+ peer-reviewed papers (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed). Use the `search` tool to look up papers for a scientific query; it takes plain-language queries and returns ranked paper records. When presenting search results, you MUST cite papers inline using their numbered references from the tool result (e.g. [1], [2], [3]). When discussing findings, always attribute them to specific papers: 'Caffeine improves endurance performance [1] and reduces perceived exertion [3].' At the end of your response, list all cited papers as numbered references with their titles hyperlinked to the URLs from the tool result: [1] [Paper Title](url) (Authors, Year, Journal, Citations). Use the exact paper URLs from the tool result — do not modify, shorten, or regenerate them. Do not omit paper links or summarize results without citing specific papers. IMPORTANT: Some search results end with a sign-up, upgrade, or usage message. When a result has one, you MUST include it at the END of your response word-for-word: do not omit, shorten, or rephrase it. When a result has none, do not add one: never write your own upgrade prompt, search count, or Consensus link. Batch at most 3 search calls at a time to avoid rate limits. For a broad request (a review, screening, finding everything on a topic), make one search with a large page_size rather than many narrower searches. If you receive a rate limit error, wait 30 seconds before retrying. Do NOT apply search filters (year_min, year_max, study_types, domain, human, sample_size_min, sjr_max, controlled, sjr_min, citation_min, open_access, country) unless the user explicitly requests them or clearly expresses intent to narrow results. If the user asks a research question without mentioning filtering criteria, call search with only the query parameter.

cockpit: 23

The routine started you with a payload: the `<routine-fire-payload>` block
below the saved prompt. Its lines say what to do; this file says how to read
them. Report to SpeedDev through the cockpit skill (`SKILL.md` next to this
file) and nothing else.

## Cockpit version

The `cockpit:` line at the top of this file is the version of the cockpit
files in this repo; the payload's `cockpit:` line is the routine's. When the
payload's number is higher, these files are older than the routine, and
every payload except for a "SpeedDev test" one does this:

1. First post one milestone (skill, "Decisions and milestones",
   `"art":"meilenstein"`) on the payload's `work item:`, with `<own>` and
   `<payload>` filled in:
   "Cockpit plugin outdated (plugin <own>, routine <payload>): sync the speeddev marketplace under claude.ai Customize > Plugins, or download the cockpit plugin again from the setup page and upload it to claude.ai."
2. Then carry on as far as these files allow.

A payload without a `cockpit:` line, or with a number that is not higher,
needs nothing.

## The payload's first line

- **"SpeedDev handover"**: read `roles/<role>.md` next to this file, where
  `<role>` is the value of the payload's `role:` line, and follow it for the
  ticket, work item and base branch the payload names.
- **"SpeedDev task"**: read `roles/free-task.md` next to this file and follow

- **"SpeedDev triage"**: read `roles/triage.md` next to this file and
  follow it for the work item, project and run the payload names. It writes
  nothing to GitHub and changes nothing in the repo.
- **"SpeedDev test"**: it only checks this setup and skips the outdated
  report above. Report exactly one milestone through the skill (its
  "Decisions and milestones"): "Cloud session test reached SpeedDev." on the
  work item its `work item:` line names. Then end the session. Change nothing
  in the repo.
- **Any other first line**: these files do not know it. Post one
  `meilenstein` on the payload's `work item:`:
  "Unknown payload "<first line>": sync the speeddev marketplace under claude.ai Customize > Plugins, or download the cockpit plugin again from the setup page and upload it to claude.ai."
  Then end the session without changing anything in the repo. Without a
  `work item:` line, end without a report.
======
# Role: end-to-end

You take a GitHub issue in state `idea` or `create-spec` from spec to
deployed, every phase in this one session. The handover payload arrives
inside `<routine-fire-payload>`; act on these lines:

- `ticket:` the issue to deliver (`owner/repo#12`).
- `work item:` your cockpit work item.
- `base branch:` branch your PR starts from and targets.
- `comment:` the person's note for this handover, if present; follow it.

## Deliver

Move the issue's `status:` label as each phase starts (exactly one, never
through a `transition` request): `create-spec`, `in-planning`, `impl`,
`in-review`, `in-test`, `ready-for-deployment`, `done`.

1. Spec: read the issue and the code it touches, then write
   `docs/specs/<issue>-<slug>.md` (goal, non-goals, decisions with reasons,
   acceptance, open questions). `<slug>` is the issue title in lower-case
   words joined by `-`.
2. Plan: write `docs/plans/<issue>-<slug>.md`, small tasks in order, each
   with its files, tests and commit.
3. Submit spec and plan together as one `draft` request and build only after
   the approval; conditions in the answer bind.
4. Build test first on a new branch off the base branch, task by task. Run
   the repo's checks before each commit. Open one PR to the base branch
   with spec, plan and code (`gh api -X POST` as in the skill's "GitHub writes"),
   its description containing `Closes #n`.
5. Review: let a fresh subagent review the diff against the spec with the
   code-review skill. Fix the findings and post the review as a PR comment.
   When a third fix round still leaves findings, ask the manager a
   `question` instead of going on.
6. Test: check every acceptance point of the spec (tests, and the running
   app where the spec asks for it) and list each with its result in the PR
   description.
7. Merge: when every check is green, ask with a `merge` request. After the
   approval, merge the PR yourself as `merging.md` next to the skill
   says, never with `gh pr merge`, and report the result on the request.
   Then watch the run with read-only `gh`: `gh run list --branch <base
   branch> --limit 1` names it, `gh run watch` follows it. A red run is a
   `blocker` with its link: leave the label at `ready-for-deployment` and
   pause.

Setting the label and commenting on the issue are routine steps: do them
yourself with the commands under "GitHub writes" in the skill and report
them afterwards. Replying to PR reviews and merging go through a request.

The manager answers a request within minutes, but one it puts to the user
can take hours. A session that stopped waiting fetches the answer at its
next hook; finish what you can meanwhile.

A paused work item resumes with a new end-to-end handover from whatever
state the label is in: the user hands it over from the card, or the manager
on the user's message, say once the merge is decided. The routine keeps the
label and gives the new session the same work item, so an approved merge
request nobody fetched arrives at its first hook: read the handoff note and
go on from that phase.

End state: `done`, or `ready-for-deployment` where the base branch has no
deploy run. Complete with `erledigt` once the run is green, or with
`pausiert` while the merge is open or the run failed: through the cockpit
(`/abschluss`) with a handoff note (`uebergabe`), as on every pause; a
reclaimed session may send no end event, and an unfinished item blocks the
next handover of this role.

content.content:
# Spec: Bacteria Wars friend links and game invites only open the app; multiplayer games cannot connect

Issue: [#3148](https://github.com/WolfSoko/wol-sok-mono/issues/3148)

## Goal

Follow the three user reports to their causes and fix the ones the game's code
can fix:

1. Friend links (`#friend=<token>`) have no effect: following one only opens
   the app.
2. Friend invites to games (challenges) have no effect besides opening the
   app.
3. Multiplayer games cannot connect.

## Analysis

The invite and challenge code works on a fresh page load:
`apps/bacteria-game-remote/e2e/online-social.spec.ts` opens an invitation
link in a new page and plays a challenge, and `online.spec.ts` connects two
devices. These failures happen only on real devices, for two reasons:

- **A. A link into the running app is never read.** `OnlineFlow.start()`
  (`libs/features/lazy/bacteria-game/src/lib/flow/online-flow.ts`) reads
  `document.location.hash` once, when the stage starts (`takeChallenge`,
  `takeInvite`). A link that opens the game while it is already running is a
  same-document navigation that changes only the fragment: in the Android
  app (the Trusted Web Activity hands the link to its open Chrome tab), in
  an installed PWA window that captures the link, or in an open tab. No
  code reads the new hash, so the player only sees the app come to the
  front. That is report 1, and it applies to a shared run's link too.
- **B. Devices behind strict NATs cannot connect.** `peer-link.ts` uses
  public STUN servers only, with no TURN relay (ADR 0009), and stops
  gathering ICE candidates after 3 s, so the offer or answer can go out
  without the server-reflexive candidate a slow mobile network brings
  later. Two phones on mobile data, or behind some Wi-Fi networks, cannot
  reach each other. The player is then told "Could not connect. Try
  again - on the same Wi-Fi it works best.", the same text as for every
  other failure. That is report 3. A friend's challenge joins the room
  through the same connection (`OnlineFlow.playChallenge` calls
  `OnlineMatchService.join`), so report 2 is most likely B as well: the
  challenge opens the online lobby, and the connection then fails.
- **C. Two devices on the same Wi-Fi fail too** (the user's own test). On
  a LAN the host candidates should connect, but Chrome hides the local IP
  behind an mDNS name (`<uuid>.local`), and the other device has to
  resolve it by multicast. Mesh, guest and client-isolated Wi-Fi networks
  often block that, and the server-reflexive fallback then needs the
  router to hairpin (send a packet to its own public address back into
  the LAN), which many home routers do not do for UDP. The e2e
  (`online.spec.ts`) launches Chromium with
  `--disable-features=WebRtcHideLocalIpsWithMdns`, so it never exercises
  this path. Without TURN the game cannot reach such a pair: only a
  relay gets through. On top of that, in matchmaking the host's
  `JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS` (20 s) ran from the claim, not from the guest's
  answer, so it dropped a link that was still connecting (the guest's
  read, candidate wait and answer all counted against it), and the
  link's own `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` never got its turn.

## Scope of this PR (step 1 of the issue)

- A: every new link hash is taken while the game runs, not only the first.
- B, part 1: a longer candidate wait, a notice of its own when the other
  device cannot be reached, and the failure's kind in analytics.
- C, part 1: the matchmaking host's join timeout covers only the wait for
  the guest's answer; a guest who answered gets the link's connect time
  once more before the host goes back to the search.

## Non-goals

- A TURN relay (B and C, part 2). The user chose Cloudflare TURN, as a
  second PR of this issue, with its own spec and plan: short-lived
  credentials from a Cloud Function, the secret, a privacy policy
  paragraph and an ADR that supersedes the "no TURN" part of ADR 0009.
  This PR says "Part of #3148".
- Push notifications for challenges while the friend is not in the game.
- Changes to the Android app: the TWA already passes the link's URL,
  fragment included, to Chrome.

## Decisions

- **Watch `hashchange` on the window rather than every router
  navigation.** A fragment that changes from outside (link capture,
  address bar, back and forward) fires `hashchange`. The game's own
  `dropHash` goes through `router.navigateByUrl(…, { replaceUrl: true })`,
  which calls `history.replaceState` and fires no `hashchange`, so taking a
  link cannot trigger itself. The manager's answer asked for the router's
  navigations; `hashchange` covers the same navigations (the router reacts
  to the same `popstate` and `hashchange`), and the game's own navigations
  don't feed back into it. A link to another path of the game (say from
  `/privacy` to `/#friend=…`) creates the stage anew, and `start()` already
  reads that hash.
- **One entry point, `takeLink()`,** runs the shared-run check and the
  invitation check on the current hash, both at start and on each
  `hashchange`. A hash that is neither does nothing, as today.
- **An invitation that arrives during a match** waits in `inviteOffer` as
  it does today. The notices show on the menu screens.
- **Candidate wait 5 s** (`GATHER_TIMEOUT_MS`, was 3 s). Gathering usually
  completes well before that, so the wait only gets longer on a network
  that really is slow.
- **The handshake's failure is typed.** `PeerLink.opened` rejects with a
  `PeerUnreachableError` whose `kind` is `ice_failed` (the connection state
  went `failed`) or `timeout` (`CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` passed without an open
  channel). A close for any other reason (the other side left, or the
  attempt was abandoned) keeps the plain error. `PeerTransport`'s docs name
  the error, and `pairedTransport()` can produce it in specs.
- **A notice of its own:** `online.notices.unreachable`, in English and
  German: "Could not reach the other device. Some mobile and Wi-Fi networks
  block direct connections - try another network, such as the same Wi-Fi."
  `online.notices.failed` stays for every other failure.
- **Analytics:** `online_ended` gets the parameter `failure` (`ice_failed`,
  `timeout` or `none`), and `docs/analytics.md` shows it. It carries no
  personal data. The privacy policy's section 11 already covers it ("how
  the connection came about and ended").

## Acceptance

1. With the game running, setting the address's hash to `#friend=<token>`
   offers the inviter, and the hash leaves the address (unit spec on
   `OnlineFlow`, simulating a same-document navigation with `hashchange`).
2. The same holds for a shared run's hash (unit spec).
3. The game's own `dropHash` does not take the link a second time (unit
   spec: `readInvite` is called once).
4. The existing invitation specs (offer, address moved on, read failure
   kept) still pass, and so does the e2e "an invitation link makes two
   players friends".
5. A connection whose ICE state goes `failed`, or that never opens within
   `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`, ends with `online.notices.unreachable` and
   `online_ended` `{ failure: 'ice_failed' | 'timeout' }`. Every other
   failure keeps `online.notices.failed` with `failure: 'none'` (unit specs
   on `OnlineMatchService` with `pairedTransport()`).
6. `GATHER_TIMEOUT_MS` is 5000.
7. `docs/analytics.md` lists `failure` on `online_ended`.
8. In matchmaking, a host whose claimed guest has answered (`connecting`)
   is not dropped when `JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS` passes; one still `waiting` for
   the answer is, as before, and one still `connecting` after
   `JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS` plus `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` is left too (unit specs on
   `MatchmakerService`).
9. `nx test`, `lint`, `lint-templates` and `typecheck-specs` of
   `feat-lazy-bacteria-game` are green, and so is the game's e2e in CI.

## Open questions

- TURN relay: decided (Cloudflare, second PR), see the non-goals.

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-10-22
- Scope: `libs/features/lazy/bacteria-game`, `apps/bacteria-game-remote`

host-authoritative: one device runs the simulation (the GPU one allowed) and
streams the owner grid to the other, which only sends its crosshair.

one seed per match through the simulation, the pellets and the bots, an

same bit. Streaming state would need a state codec, a guest-side stand-in
for the simulation and the engine (HUD, sound events, outcome, minimap all
read the engine) and a painter path for received state.

(ADR 0007), so a place for two devices to meet costs nothing new.

**Lockstep on the CPU simulation.** Both devices run the same `MatchEngine`
with the same seed; each tick is played only once both seats' inputs for it
are in. What a player puts in is played `INPUT_DELAY_TICKS` (6, 100 ms)
later on both devices, so it usually arrives before the other device needs
it; when it does not, that device waits rather than guesses. Both seats are
driven through the engine's seat drivers (`SeatDriver`, which the ghost
already implements), so the engine needed no new code path. Online matches
run on the CPU simulation at the _Normal_ grid on both devices, whatever
their settings, and only on base-size maps.

checksum of the players (colony sizes, scores, crosshairs); should they
differ, the match ends as "out of step". The CPU simulation uses a handful

it visible if it ever happens.

room `rooms/{code}` (six letters and digits) with its offer, the guest
writes its answer into it; offers and answers carry all their ICE
candidates, so each side writes one string. The rules let anyone signed in
read a room by its code but not list rooms, and only one guest answer one.

and reliable: inputs are a few dozen bytes 60 times a second. Without a

colours and starts every match (sending the seed); the guest follows. A

  online. Lifting either means the host-authoritative design after all.

# Spec: Bacteria Wars friend links and game invites only open the app; multiplayer games cannot connect

Issue: [#3148](https://github.com/WolfSoko/wol-sok-mono/issues/3148)

## Goal

Follow the three user reports to their causes and fix the ones the game's code
can fix:

1. Friend links (`#friend=<token>`) have no effect: following one only opens
   the app.
2. Friend invites to games (challenges) have no effect besides opening the
   app.
3. Multiplayer games cannot connect.

## Analysis

The invite and challenge code works on a fresh page load:
`apps/bacteria-game-remote/e2e/online-social.spec.ts` opens an invitation
link in a new page and plays a challenge, and `online.spec.ts` connects two
devices. These failures happen only on real devices, for two reasons:

- **A. A link into the running app is never read.** `OnlineFlow.start()`
  (`libs/features/lazy/bacteria-game/src/lib/flow/online-flow.ts`) reads
  `document.location.hash` once, when the stage starts (`takeChallenge`,
  `takeInvite`). A link that opens the game while it is already running is a
  same-document navigation that changes only the fragment: in the Android
  app (the Trusted Web Activity hands the link to its open Chrome tab), in
  an installed PWA window that captures the link, or in an open tab. No
  code reads the new hash, so the player only sees the app come to the
  front. That is report 1, and it applies to a shared run's link too.
- **B. Devices behind strict NATs cannot connect.** `peer-link.ts` uses
  public STUN servers only, with no TURN relay (ADR 0009), and stops
  gathering ICE candidates after 3 s, so the offer or answer can go out
  without the server-reflexive candidate a slow mobile network brings
  later. Two phones on mobile data, or behind some Wi-Fi networks, cannot
  reach each other. The player is then told "Could not connect. Try
  again - on the same Wi-Fi it works best.", the same text as for every
  other failure. That is report 3. A friend's challenge joins the room
  through the same connection (`OnlineFlow.playChallenge` calls
  `OnlineMatchService.join`), so report 2 is most likely B as well: the
  challenge opens the online lobby, and the connection then fails.
- **C. Two devices on the same Wi-Fi fail too** (the user's own test). On
  a LAN the host candidates should connect, but Chrome hides the local IP
  behind an mDNS name (`<uuid>.local`), and the other device has to
  resolve it by multicast. Mesh, guest and client-isolated Wi-Fi networks
  often block that, and the server-reflexive fallback then needs the
  router to hairpin (send a packet to its own public address back into
  the LAN), which many home routers do not do for UDP. The e2e
  (`online.spec.ts`) launches Chromium with
  `--disable-features=WebRtcHideLocalIpsWithMdns`, so it never exercises
  this path. Without TURN the game cannot reach such a pair: only a
  relay gets through. On top of that, in matchmaking the host's
  `JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS` (20 s) ran from the claim, not from the guest's
  answer, so it dropped a link that was still connecting (the guest's
  read, candidate wait and answer all counted against it), and the
  link's own `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` never got its turn.

## Scope of this PR (step 1 of the issue)

- A: every new link hash is taken while the game runs, not only the first.
- B, part 1: a longer candidate wait, a notice of its own when the other
  device cannot be reached, and the failure's kind in analytics.
- C, part 1: the matchmaking host's join timeout covers only the wait for
  the guest's answer; a guest who answered gets the link's connect time
  once more before the host goes back to the search.

## Non-goals

- A TURN relay (B and C, part 2). The user chose Cloudflare TURN, as a
  second PR of this issue, with its own spec and plan: short-lived
  credentials from a Cloud Function, the secret, a privacy policy
  paragraph and an ADR that supersedes the "no TURN" part of ADR 0009.
  This PR says "Part of #3148".
- Push notifications for challenges while the friend is not in the game.
- Changes to the Android app: the TWA already passes the link's URL,
  fragment included, to Chrome.

## Decisions

- **Watch `hashchange` on the window rather than every router
  navigation.** A fragment that changes from outside (link capture,
  address bar, back and forward) fires `hashchange`. The game's own
  `dropHash` goes through `router.navigateByUrl(…, { replaceUrl: true })`,
  which calls `history.replaceState` and fires no `hashchange`, so taking a
  link cannot trigger itself. The manager's answer asked for the router's
  navigations; `hashchange` covers the same navigations (the router reacts
  to the same `popstate` and `hashchange`), and the game's own navigations
  don't feed back into it. A link to another path of the game (say from
  `/privacy` to `/#friend=…`) creates the stage anew, and `start()` already
  reads that hash.
- **One entry point, `takeLink()`,** runs the shared-run check and the
  invitation check on the current hash, both at start and on each
  `hashchange`. A hash that is neither does nothing, as today.
- **An invitation that arrives during a match** waits in `inviteOffer` as
  it does today. The notices show on the menu screens.
- **Candidate wait 5 s** (`GATHER_TIMEOUT_MS`, was 3 s). Gathering usually
  completes well before that, so the wait only gets longer on a network
  that really is slow.
- **The handshake's failure is typed.** `PeerLink.opened` rejects with a
  `PeerUnreachableError` whose `kind` is `ice_failed` (the connection state
  went `failed`) or `timeout` (`CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` passed without an open
  channel). A close for any other reason (the other side left, or the
  attempt was abandoned) keeps the plain error. `PeerTransport`'s docs name
  the error, and `pairedTransport()` can produce it in specs.
- **A notice of its own:** `online.notices.unreachable`, in English and
  German: "Could not reach the other device. Some mobile and Wi-Fi networks
  block direct connections - try another network, such as the same Wi-Fi."
  `online.notices.failed` stays for every other failure.
- **Analytics:** `online_ended` gets the parameter `failure` (`ice_failed`,
  `timeout` or `none`), and `docs/analytics.md` shows it. It carries no
  personal data. The privacy policy's section 11 already covers it ("how
  the connection came about and ended").

## Acceptance

1. With the game running, setting the address's hash to `#friend=<token>`
   offers the inviter, and the hash leaves the address (unit spec on
   `OnlineFlow`, simulating a same-document navigation with `hashchange`).
2. The same holds for a shared run's hash (unit spec).
3. The game's own `dropHash` does not take the link a second time (unit
   spec: `readInvite` is called once).
4. The existing invitation specs (offer, address moved on, read failure
   kept) still pass, and so does the e2e "an invitation link makes two
   players friends".
5. A connection whose ICE state goes `failed`, or that never opens within
   `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`, ends with `online.notices.unreachable` and
   `online_ended` `{ failure: 'ice_failed' | 'timeout' }`. Every other
   failure keeps `online.notices.failed` with `failure: 'none'` (unit specs
   on `OnlineMatchService` with `pairedTransport()`).
6. `GATHER_TIMEOUT_MS` is 5000.
7. `docs/analytics.md` lists `failure` on `online_ended`.
8. In matchmaking, a host whose claimed guest has answered (`connecting`)
   is not dropped when `JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS` passes; one still `waiting` for
   the answer is, as before, and one still `connecting` after
   `JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS` plus `CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` is left too (unit specs on
   `MatchmakerService`).
9. `nx test`, `lint`, `lint-templates` and `typecheck-specs` of
   `feat-lazy-bacteria-game` are green, and so is the game's e2e in CI.

## Open questions

- TURN relay: decided (Cloudflare, second PR), see the non-goals.
- Whether the failing links were opened with the app already running, and
  whether the failing matches were on mobile data: to be asked of the user
  next. The spec goes ahead on the analysis either way.
